title: A plugin's descriptor
description:
What a plugin published to the Orknux marketplace says about itself.

A plugin is published as a .js file, as a .zip of that file and the libraries beside it, or by giving the address of such a zip on GitHub. A zip may carry this descriptor at its top level, and it must be named `plugin.json`. One name and not several: an archive carrying two spellings of the same thing would leave which one won to a line of code rather than to anything its author can see.

**The descriptor wins over the publish form.** The form fills what the descriptor does not say, and not the other way round -- which matters most when editing, because the edit form arrives prefilled with the listing as it stands, so a form that beat the descriptor would mean a new zip could never change a version. To change what a listing says, change this file.

It is the same shape orknux-extension gives each of its plugins, one `plugin.json` per folder, so a plugin's folder zipped straight out of that repository needs nothing typed at all.

This is prose and nothing more. The marketplace does not read what a plugin will ask to be allowed and does not vouch for it: permissions, capabilities and the libraries it ships with are discovered by the installing server from the code itself, in its sandbox, at the moment somebody accepts them -- and so is what it offers, its functions, tools, skills, types and the workflow actions an Action node can be pointed at. The one claim checked here is `key`, because a listing keyed differently from what the code answers is a listing that installs as something else.

key.description: The plugin's own id -- what `id()` answers. It is the address on this site, and what ties the listing to an installed row on the server that takes it, so it never changes once published. Checked against the source: where `id()` can be read out of the uploaded file and disagrees with this, the upload is refused rather than listed under a name it will not install as.

name.description: The human name, for the list.

summary.description: One line, shown beside the name. Not the first line of the description: this is read in a list of twenty things.

version.description:
The offering's own string. The marketplace neither parses nor compares these -- a server that wants to say 'update available' compares against what it recorded at install.

**A version is a release.** Publishing a key that already exists replaces its listing, keeping its reviews and its download count, and records the version in that plugin's history. Republishing the same number does not add a second entry: it leaves the listing's place in 'newest first' alone, so correcting a typo in the summary is not an announcement. Where the bytes move under a number that did not, the history says so -- that is a plugin edited without being renumbered, and it is worth avoiding.

The ten newest releases keep their files, so somebody can take the version they had rather than only the current one. Older releases stay in the history without their bytes.

author.description: Who wrote it, for display. Advisory only: the listing's author is the account that published it, which is the one thing here nobody can type.

tags.description:
What the plugin is for, in your own words -- `chat`, `files`, `search`. The marketplace filters by these.

A list, because a plugin is usually more than one thing: filing the Slack plugin under only `chat` hides it from everybody looking for the plugin that carries files.

Free text rather than a list to choose from, so look at what the marketplace already shows before inventing a word -- a tag only one plugin uses is a filter that finds one plugin. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens; at most eight. Absent is a plugin that appears under everything and under no filter.

icon.description: The plugin's icon for a **light** ground: the path to an SVG inside the archive, relative to the plugin's own folder. Defaults to `icon.svg` where the archive has one. Where a file of the same name with a `-white` suffix sits beside it -- `icon.svg` and `icon-white.svg` -- that second one is taken as the same glyph in white, for a dark ground. Only the first is named here; the other is found by that suffix, so a plugin shipping one icon says nothing and a plugin shipping both says nothing either. Give each a real colour on a fill or a stroke. `currentColor` looks tempting and does not work: an SVG loaded through `` is its own document, inherits no colour from the page, and resolves `currentColor` to black -- an empty square on a dark listing. That is the whole reason there are two files rather than one clever one. Refused rather than sanitized, both of them: an SVG carrying a script, an event handler, a foreignObject, an iframe, an XML entity declaration or a `javascript:` reference is not published. It would be served from the origin that holds everybody's session, and a scrubber that misses one of those is worse than no icon. At most 64 KB each.

descriptionPath.description: Which file in the archive holds the long description, as markdown, relative to the plugin's own folder. Defaults to `README.md`, which is where every plugin in the extension repository keeps it. The markdown is passed through as written and rendered by whoever shows it -- somebody else's prose from an upload, so the shower sanitizes.

path.description: Which file in the archive is the plugin itself, relative to its own folder -- `greeter.js`. Only needed where the archive has more than one .js at its top level, which is otherwise refused as a guess nobody could check. A single-file upload is its own answer.

examples.name: Greeter
